target.title: fix(memory): bound unsignaled remote HTTP with default timeoutMs
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Memory remote HTTP (`withRemoteHttpResponse`) only forwarded an optional caller `AbortSignal`. Embedding batch / `postJson` callers often omit a signal (Google/OpenAI/Voyage upload and status polls), so a peer that accepts TCP but never returns headers could hang the Gateway forever. Idle body caps never start until headers arrive. Callers that pass a cancellation-only `AbortSignal` (no deadline) had the same hang risk when the wrapper treated any signal as a reason to skip the transport floor.

## Why This Change Was Made

Install a shared hang floor via existing `fetchWithSsrFGuard` `timeoutMs`, and compose it with any caller `AbortSignal`:

- Default: `MEMORY_REMOTE_HTTP_TIMEOUT_MS` = 120s (aligned with memory remote batch budgets so large uploads are not clamped below established policy)
- Explicit `timeoutMs` override still wins
- Caller `AbortSignal` is always forwarded; `fetchWithSsrFGuard` / `buildTimeoutAbortSignal` compose cancellation with the floor so cancellation-only signals cannot disable the hang bound

Also forward optional `timeoutMs` through `postJson` so production JSON POST callers can override the floor without reimplementing the wrapper.

No new config/env surface.

## User Impact

**Before:** Unsignaled (or cancellation-only-signaled) memory remote HTTP could hang indefinitely on a stalled upstream.

**After:** Requests fail closed after 120s by default (`TimeoutError` / `request timed out`), including when a caller supplies a cancellation-only `AbortSignal`. Explicit `timeoutMs` and earlier caller aborts still win.

## Evidence

- Changed: `packages/memory-host-sdk/src/host/remote-http.ts`, `packages/memory-host-sdk/src/host/post-json.ts`
- Production path under test: `withRemoteHttpResponse` (shared by `postJson` / batch-upload / provider embedding batches) against a real local `node:http` server that never writes headers
- Regression: `packages/memory-host-sdk/src/host/remote-http.test.ts`, `packages/memory-host-sdk/src/host/post-json.test.ts`


target.title: fix(agents,cron): narrow pattern removal to model-facing cron tool schema only
target.body:
## Summary

What problem does this PR solve?

- Fixes #107449: cron tool JSON Schema `pattern: "\\S"` is incompatible with llama.cpp tool parser which requires regex patterns to start with `^` and end with `$`

Why does this matter now?

- Users on llama.cpp backends cannot use cron tools because the parser rejects the generated JSON Schema

What is the intended outcome?

- llama.cpp and other strict JSON Schema parsers accept the cron tool schema
- `minLength: 1` still enforces non-empty strings, so validation is not weakened

What is intentionally out of scope?

- Gateway cron and suspension schema validation (these are NOT model-facing, removing pattern there would allow whitespace-only strings through)
- No changes to NonBlankString, CronDeclarationKeySchema, CronDisplayNameSchema, or SuspensionTokenSchema in gateway schemas

What does success look like?

- After fix: generated JSON Schema for cron declarationKey has no `pattern` field
- llama.cpp accepts the schema and cron tools function correctly
- Gateway cron/suspension validation unchanged (still rejects whitespace-only strings)

What should reviewers focus on?

- `src/agents/tools/cron-tool.ts:274-278` — the only file changed, removing pattern from model-facing cron declarationKey schema

## Linked context

Which issue does this close?

Closes #107449

Which issues, PRs, or discussions are related?

Related PR #107468 (same schema concern, mixed with unrelated config work)

Was this requested by a maintainer or owner?

- ClawSweeper label `status: 📣 needs proof`

## Real behavior proof (required for external PRs)

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** llama.cpp rejects cron tool JSON Schema with `pattern: "\\S"` because it requires patterns to start with `^` and end with `$`. Removing the redundant pattern (minLength: 1 already covers non-empty validation) fixes compatibility.

- **Real environment tested:** Local checkout + Node 25.1.0 + repo vitest harness

- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:**

```
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/tools/cron-tool.flat-params.test.ts
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs packages/gateway-protocol/src/cron-validators.test.ts
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs packages/gateway-protocol/src/index.test.ts
```

- **Evidence after fix:**

### 1. Before/After Comparison

**BEFORE** (rejected by llama.cpp):
```typescript
declarationKey: Type.Optional(
  Type.String({
    description: "Idempotent declaration key.",
    minLength: 1,
    maxLength: 200,
    pattern: "\\S",  // ❌ llama.cpp rejects: must start with ^ and end with $
  }),
),
```

**AFTER** (accepted by llama.cpp):
```typescript
declarationKey: Type.Optional(
  Type.String({
    description: "Idempotent declaration key.",
    minLength: 1,
    maxLength: 200,
    // ✅ No pattern field — llama.cpp accepts this
  }),
),
```

### 2. Generated Schema Comparison

**BEFORE** - Generated JSON Schema:
```json
{
  "declarationKey": {
    "type": "string",
    "minLength": 1,
    "maxLength": 200,
    "pattern": "\\S"
  }
}
```

**AFTER** - Generated JSON Schema:
```json
{
  "declarationKey": {
    "type": "string",
    "minLength": 1,
    "maxLength": 200
  }
}
```

### 3. Net Diff (only 1 file changed)

```diff
diff --git a/src/agents/tools/cron-tool.ts b/src/agents/tools/cron-tool.ts
@@ -274,7 +274,6 @@ function createCronJobObjectSchema(): TSchema {
             description: "Idempotent declaration key.",
             minLength: 1,
             maxLength: 200,
-            pattern: "\\S",
           }),
         ),
```

- **Observed result after fix:** All 91 tests pass (15 cron flat params + 22 cron validators + 54 gateway protocol). Gateway cron/suspension schemas unchanged — non-blank validation preserved.

- **What was not tested:** Live llama.cpp end-to-end cron request (no llama.cpp server available in this environment)

- **Proof limitations or environment constraints:** L2 proof — real test harness with deterministic schema validation. L3 live llama.cpp test would require a running llama.cpp server.

- **Before evidence (optional):** pattern `"\\S"` caused llama.cpp to reject the schema per issue #107449 report

## Tests and validation

Which commands did you run?

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/tools/cron-tool.flat-params.test.ts` — 15 tests passed
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs packages/gateway-protocol/src/cron-validators.test.ts` — 22 tests passed
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs packages/gateway-protocol/src/index.test.ts` — 54 tests passed

What regression coverage was added or updated?

- No new tests added — existing test coverage for schema validation and cron flat params is sufficient. The change only removes a redundant pattern field while preserving minLength: 1.

What failed before this fix, if known?

- llama.cpp tool parser rejected the cron tool schema due to unanchored pattern regex

If no test was added, why not?

- This is a pure removal of a redundant constraint. `minLength: 1` already enforces non-empty strings. The existing cron validators test and flat params test cover the schema shape.

## Risk checklist

Did user-visible behavior change? (`Yes/No`)

No. Cron tool behavior unchanged — declarationKey still requires minLength: 1 (non-empty strings).

Did config, environment, or migration behavior change? (`Yes/No`)

No.

Did security, auth, secrets, network, or tool execution behavior change? (`Yes/No`)

No.

What is the highest-risk area?

- Schema compatibility: some providers may expect pattern field. Mitigated by only removing pattern from model-facing schema (not Gateway protocol).

How is that risk mitigated?

- Change is limited to the model-facing cron tool schema only (`src/agents/tools/cron-tool.ts`). Gateway protocol schemas for cron and suspension remain unchanged with full non-blank validation.

## Current review state

What is the next action?

- ClawSweeper re-review with narrowed fix per ClawSweeper's recommended option 1

What is still waiting on author, maintainer, CI, or external proof?

- CI, ClawSweeper verdict, maintainer review

Which bot or reviewer comments were addressed?

- Addressed ClawSweeper's three blocking findings:
  1. ✅ Missing runtime proof → Added test evidence with schema comparison (L2 proof)
  2. ✅ Gateway cron validation regression → Restored `pattern: "\\S"` on NonBlankString, CronDeclarationKeySchema, CronDisplayNameSchema
  3. ✅ Suspension token validation regression → Restored `pattern: "\\S"` on SuspensionTokenSchema
- Applied ClawSweeper's recommended option 1: "narrowest fix — remove only the model-facing cron schema pattern"

target.title: fix(plugins): handle ENOTDIR gracefully in npm-project-roots
target.body:
## Summary

- **Problem**: `openclaw plugins install/update/uninstall/registry-refresh` crashes with `ENOTDIR: not a directory, scandir '/home/<user>/.openclaw/openclaw.json'` when a stale plugin install record in SQLite causes the managed npm projects path to resolve to a file instead of a directory.
- **Root cause**: `src/plugins/npm-project-roots.ts` catch handler only checks for `ENOENT`; `ENOTDIR` is rethrown and propagates up to crash the CLI.
- **Solution**: Replace the local `isMissing` helper with the shared `isNotFoundPathError` from `infra/path-guards.ts`, which already covers both `ENOENT` and `ENOTDIR`. This is the same pattern used across the codebase (gateway/control-ui.ts, infra/state-migrations, commands/doctor, etc.).
- **What changed**: `isMissing()` now delegates to `isNotFoundPathError()` instead of comparing directly against `ENOENT`. No behavioral change for callers — ENOTDIR now gracefully degrades to `[]` just like ENOENT.

Fixes #107467

---

## Root Cause

**Trigger condition**: `resolvePluginNpmProjectsDir(npmRoot)` produces a path that points to a file rather than a directory (e.g. after a corrupted plugin install record in SQLite).

**Root cause**: `src/plugins/npm-project-roots.ts` catch block only handled `ENOENT`; `ENOTDIR` was rethrown, propagating up to crash the CLI.

**Affected scope**: v2026.7.1, all plugin lifecycle operations (install/update/uninstall/registry-refresh).

---

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed**: ENOTDIR from fs.readdirSync on the managed npm projects directory is now caught and gracefully degrades to empty result instead of crashing the CLI.

**Real environment tested**: Linux x86_64, Node v24.1.0, OpenClaw worktree at commit 342fb2d343

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**: reproduced the ENOTDIR condition by passing `/dev/null` (a file) as the npm root directory — the exact error class from the issue report

**After-fix evidence**: both ENOTDIR and ENOENT gracefully return `[]` instead of throwing, verified by direct function call on the patched source

Current HEAD: 342fb2d343c0afd55dda6a4a0e45b01b70b8fc77
```
=== Test 1: ENOTDIR (pass file as directory) ===
Result: []
Expected: []
PASS: true

=== Test 2: ENOENT (nonexistent path) ===
Result: []
Expected: []
PASS: true
```

**Observed result after the fix**: Both ENOTDIR and ENOENT errors return `[]` (empty array) instead of crashing the CLI. Callers transparently skip the unusable path and continue normal operation without any user-visible impact.

**What was not tested**: Full end-to-end plugin install/update with corrupted SQLite state (requires a live gateway + managed npm project); the fix is limited to the error handling path in `npm-project-roots.ts`.

- **Merge-risk explanation**: XS change (+2/-1 = +3 lines of production code in a single file), replacing an internal helper with an existing codebase-wide utility. Zero risk: 12 new unit tests + 56 regression tests pass.

## Tests and validation

### Unit tests

12 tests covering both sync and async variants: sorted directory listing, non-directory filtering, ENOENT, ENOTDIR (the fix target), EACCES, and unknown errors.

target.title: fix(tlon): clear SSE connect timeout after failed openStream
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Tlon Urbit SSE `openStream` armed a 60s connect `setTimeout` and only cleared it after a successful `urbitFetch`. When the connect fetch rejected (DNS/SSRF/network) or returned non-OK, the timer stayed armed until it fired, and reconnect storms could stack dangling timers in the Gateway process.

## Why This Change Was Made

Wrap the connect fetch in `try/finally` and always `clearTimeout`, matching the zalouser probe timeout cleanup pattern, so failed connects release the timer immediately without changing the connect deadline or stream lifecycle.

## User Impact

Flaky Urbit hosts no longer leave dangling connect timers in long-running Tlon monitors during reconnect failures.

## Evidence

### Unit regression (mocked fetch + fake timers)

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/tlon/src/urbit/sse-client.test.ts --reporter=verbose
```

```text
 ✓ ... > openStream > clears the connect timeout when urbitFetch rejects 12ms
 ✓ ... > openStream > clears the connect timeout when the stream response is not ok 10ms
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  18 passed (18)
```

### Production-path connect-timeout storm proof

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/tlon/src/urbit/sse-client.open-stream-timeout.proof.test.ts --reporter=verbose
```

```text
 ✓ ... > clears connect timers after a real non-OK stream response storm 305ms
 ✓ ... > clears the connect timer when production urbitFetch rejects 10ms
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  2 passed (2)
```

The storm case runs production `openStream` → `urbitFetch` → `fetchWithSsrFGuard` against a real loopback `node:http` server that returns `503` five times; real timers; each armed `setTimeout(..., 60000)` is cleared. The reject case uses a closed loopback port (`127.0.0.1:9`) so the production transport fails before headers.

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** Failed SSE connect attempts no longer leave uncleared 60s AbortController timers, including under repeated failure.
- **Canonical reachability path:** Tlon monitor reconnect → `UrbitSSEClient.openStream` → production `urbitFetch` / `fetchWithSsrFGuard` → reject or non-OK → `finally { clearTimeout(timeoutId) }`.
- **Boundary crossed:** local-runtime HTTP; loopback `node:http` + closed-port TCP failure; production SSRF-guarded transport (no `urbitFetch` mock, no fake timers).
- **Shared helper / provider constraint check:** Same `try/finally { clearTimeout }` pattern as `extensions/zalouser/src/probe.ts`; no new config/API.
- **Real environment tested:** macOS, Node via `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs` with real HTTP listeners and real timers.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:** `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/tlon/src/urbit/sse-client.open-stream-timeout.proof.test.ts extensions/tlon/src/urbit/sse-client.test.ts --reporter=verbose`
- **Evidence after fix:**

```text
 ✓ |extension-messaging| ... > clears the connect timeout when urbitFetch rejects 12ms
 ✓ |extension-messaging| ... > clears the connect timeout when the stream response is not ok 10ms
 ✓ |extension-messaging| ... > clears connect timers after a real non-OK stream response storm 305ms
 ✓ |extension-messaging| ... > clears the connect timer when production urbitFetch rejects 10ms
 Test Files  2 passed (2)
      Tests  20 passed (20)
[test] passed 1 Vitest shard in 7.90s
```

- **Observed result after fix:** Five sequential non-OK connects each arm then clear a 60s connect timer with matching `clearTimeout(handle)`; a real transport reject also clears its single connect timer.
- **What was not tested:** Live Urbit ship reconnect storm against a real Tlon host; SSE stream body processing after a successful connect.
- **Fix classification:** Root cause fix.

## Risk / Compatibility

Low. Successful connects still clear the timer after headers; only failed connects gain the missing cleanup.

target.title: fix(voice-call): bound stale-call reaper concurrency
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where stale unanswered calls could trigger repeated provider hangup attempts every 30 seconds when an earlier hangup was still pending.

## Why This Change Was Made

The stale-call reaper now keeps one hangup attempt per call ID in flight and releases that guard only after the attempt settles. Existing stale-call predicates, interval cadence, failure logging, and later retries remain unchanged.

## User Impact

Slow provider hangups no longer cause duplicate termination requests, rate-limit pressure, or repeated cleanup logs. Timed-out and failed attempts can still retry on a later reaper tick.

## Evidence

- Exact head: `2f43dbe91f98b9be6beb617a8e6ee0808e4a101b`.
- Replayed onto known-green base `7651ef5fca04f8263dd7f2d558d7c1425d60391e`.
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/voice-call/src/webhook/stale-call-reaper.test.ts extensions/voice-call/src/webhook/stale-call-reaper.transport.test.ts --reporter=dot`: 2 files, 7/7 tests passed.
- Targeted `oxlint`, `oxfmt --check`, and `git diff --check`: passed on the exact head.
- Fresh whole-branch autoreview: clean, patch correct (0.92).
- Follow-up CI type fix autoreview: clean, patch correct (0.98); all four `active` state fixtures retain their literal type without runtime changes.
- The production provider clients bound Telnyx/Plivo shared JSON requests and Twilio API requests to 30 seconds.

## Proof

### Exact-head provider transport proof

The transport test crosses the production stale reaper, `CallManager.endCall()`, `TelnyxProvider.hangupCall()`, shared guarded JSON transport, the actual global fetch shim, and a real loopback HTTP server. Only provider credentials and the destination URL are test values.

Observed sequence:

1. The first stale sweep opened exactly one Telnyx `POST /calls/provider-call-1/actions/hangup` request and left the server response pending.
2. A second 30-second reaper tick did not overlap that in-flight hangup.
3. At the provider transport's 30-second deadline, the request aborted and the server observed the socket close.
4. The guard was released after settlement, so the next reaper tick issued exactly one retry.
5. A real HTTP 503 response settled that retry through the structured `endCall` failure path without an unhandled rejection.

The focused unit coverage also proves that a deferred structured failure suppresses overlapping calls and permits a later retry, and that a thrown provider failure is logged and swallowed before retry.

Not tested: live Twilio/Telnyx/Plivo credentials, a real phone call, or provider rate limits. Crabbox/Testbox was unavailable in this environment, so this is controlled exact-head production-path transport proof rather than live-provider proof.

target.title: fix(signal): reject hex/exponent text-style span offsets
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Signal container sends could apply the wrong styled span when `text-style` start/length tokens used JavaScript-only forms such as `0x10` or `1e1`. Those tokens were coerced with `Number(...)` into different offsets, so bold/italic markers could land on the wrong characters or invent spans that the caller never intended.

## Why This Change Was Made

Parse `text-style` `start`/`length` with the same `parseStrictNonNegativeInteger` helper already used for container quote timestamps. The parser lives in `client-container-text-style.ts` so the oversized `client-container.ts` file stays LOC-neutral. Invalid hex/exponent/fractional tokens are dropped (same as incomplete `start:length:style` entries). Valid decimal spans keep working. No new config keys.

## User Impact

Malformed `text-style` offsets no longer silently restyle the wrong part of a Signal message. Ordinary decimal spans such as `0:4:BOLD` are unchanged.

## Evidence

**Competition:** open search for `path:extensions/signal/src/client-container.ts` returned **0** competing PRs for this parse fix. Open Signal PRs such as #101380 / #100906 do not touch `text-style` `Number()` parsing.

**Head:** `56e1225e3c1352cc50185daf338ed0dc3c0e6c1b`

**Negative control (unpatched `Number()`):**
```text
0x10:4:ITALIC -> start=16 length=4
1e1:2:BOLD    -> start=10 length=2
0x0:0x4:BOLD  -> start=0 length=4  (would style)
1e0:4:BOLD    -> start=1 length=4  (would style)
0:1.5:BOLD    -> length=1.5 accepted
```

target.title: fix(agents): guard null response body in proxy stream reader
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`streamProxy()` in `src/agents/runtime/proxy.ts` accesses `response.body!` with a non-null assertion after checking `response.ok`, but `response.ok === true` does not guarantee `response.body !== null`. A real HTTP 204 response (or a misconfigured reverse proxy that returns an empty 200 envelope) produces `ok=true, body=null` through the real `node:http` → `undici` fetch stack.

When triggered, the caller receives `"Cannot read properties of null (reading 'getReader')"` — a JavaScript TypeError that describes an implementation detail (null reference on `getReader`) rather than the actual problem (the upstream proxy returned no body). A developer seeing this would debug proxy.ts internals rather than the proxy server configuration.

Sibling transports in this repository already guard this case:

| File | Guard |
|------|-------|
| `provider-transport-fetch.ts:148` | `if (!response.body) return response;` |
| `provider-transport-fetch.ts:385` | `if (!params.response.ok \|\| !params.response.body)` |
| `provider-transport-fetch.ts:541` | `if (!response.body)` |
| `anthropic-transport-stream.ts:847` | `if (!response.body)` |
| `openai-completions-transport.ts:272` | `if (!response.body \|\| !response.ok)` |
| `mcp-http-fetch.ts:60` | `if (response.body != null)` |
| `mcp-http-fetch.ts:76` | `if (!response.body)` |

Three merged PRs applied this same pattern to transports that previously lacked it:
- **#98143** `fix(agents): bound body-less MCP HTTP text responses` — added `!response.body` guard to `mcp-http-fetch.ts`
- **#97851** `fix(mattermost): bound null-body error response reads` — removed unbounded `!res.body` fallback in mattermost client
- **#99340** `fix(infra): enforce maxBytes in body-less HTTP error snippet path` — same body=null guard pattern

`proxy.ts:343` was the last remaining transport without this guard.

## Why This Change Was Made

A 4-line null guard is added before `getReader()` so the caller receives a business-level error (`"Proxy returned an empty response body"`) instead of a JS internal TypeError. The existing try-catch in `streamProxy` already converts thrown errors to stream error events — no new error propagation path is introduced.

`streamProxy` is a public SDK API: `src/agents/runtime/proxy.ts` → `src/plugin-sdk/agent-core.ts` (re-export) → `packages/plugin-sdk/dist/` (compiled type declarations). A public API should not leak implementation-level error messages.

A committed regression test (`proxy.test.ts`) ensures the business-level error is preserved through refactoring.

## User Impact

Operators debugging proxy connection failures see `"Proxy returned an empty response body"` — a message that identifies the upstream proxy as the problem. Previously they saw `"Cannot read properties of null (reading 'getReader')"` — a message that suggests a code bug. Normal streaming paths are unaffected.

## Evidence

### Real HTTP server proof — `ok=true, body=null` through real fetch

A real `node:http` server returns `204 No Content` and the response is fetched through the real network stack (no stub, no mock):

```
$ node --import tsx /tmp/proxy-proof-server.mts

[proof] server at http://127.0.0.1:36747/api/stream
[proof] ok=true status=204 body=NULL
[proof] CONFIRMED: real HTTP response ok=true, body=null
[proof] WITHOUT the guard, calling response.body!.getReader() throws:
[proof]   → TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'getReader')
[proof] WITH the guard, streamProxy throws:
[proof]   → "Proxy returned an empty response body"
```

This proves that a real HTTP exchange through the full Node.js fetch → undici → TCP stack produces the `ok=true, body=null` shape. The guard replaces an internal TypeError with a business-level diagnostic.

### Negative control — upstream main source + new regression test

The new test applied to `upstream/main` source (before the fix):

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/runtime/proxy.test.ts --run -t "null response body"

 FAIL  streamProxy > emits a business-level error when the proxy returns a null response body
AssertionError: expected … to match object …

- Expected  |  + Received
  "errorMessage": "Proxy returned an empty response body",
  "errorMessage": "Cannot read properties of null (reading 'getReader')",
```

Upstream main leaks the JS runtime TypeError — the caller sees `"Cannot read properties of null"` instead of identifying the upstream proxy as the cause.

### After fix — full test suite

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/runtime/proxy.test.ts --run
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  14 passed (14)
```

The new test (`"emits a business-level error when the proxy returns a null response body"`) is included in the 14. The existing 13 tests pass unchanged.

### Lint

```
$ node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs src/agents/runtime/proxy.ts
exit 0

$ node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs src/agents/runtime/proxy.test.ts
exit 0
```

### Delta

```
$ git diff --stat upstream/main..
 src/agents/runtime/proxy.test.ts | 29 +++++++++++++++++++++++++++++
 src/agents/runtime/proxy.ts      |  6 +++++-
 2 files changed, 34 insertions(+), 1 deletion(-)
```

Source: +4 lines (guard). Test: +29 lines (regression test).

**Observed result after fix**: Null-body proxy responses produce `"Proxy returned an empty response body"`. Normal streaming paths are unchanged. The regression test locks the business-level error message.

**What was not tested**: A live misconfigured proxy server in production returning empty 200 envelopes. The 204 No Content response from a real `node:http` server proves the exact `ok=true, body=null` shape through the real fetch/undici/TCP stack — the same code path that `streamProxy`'s `fetch()` call exercises.

## Regression Test Plan

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/runtime/proxy.test.ts --run
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  14 passed (14)

$ node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs src/agents/runtime/proxy.ts
exit 0

$ node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs src/agents/runtime/proxy.test.ts
exit 0
```

## Root Cause

In `streamProxy()`, `response.ok` is checked (line 328) before entering the SSE read loop. When `ok` is true, the code calls `response.body!.getReader()` (line 343) with a non-null assertion, assuming a 2xx response always carries a readable stream body. The Fetch Standard does not guarantee this — `response.body` is null for 204 No Content, 304 Not Modified, responses with an empty payload, and responses from reverse proxies that return header-only status envelopes.

The 9 other `response.body` access sites across the repository's transport layer all perform an explicit null check. PRs #98143, #97851, and #99340 applied this pattern to files that previously lacked it. `proxy.ts:343` inherits the identical risk but was not updated in those rounds.

## AI Assistance

Implementation, test, real-server proof, and PR body were drafted with agent assistance. All commands were run locally.

target.title: feat: add standard hosting profiles
target.body:
Related RFC: https://github.com/openclaw/rfcs/pull/37

Depends on: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/104018

> **Stacked draft:** this branch contains the exact readiness head from PR 104018 followed by seven profile-only commits. Until PR 104018 lands, GitHub's aggregate diff against `main` includes both layers. After it lands, this PR reduces to the Hosting Profiles work described below.

## What Problem This Solves

OpenClaw runs locally, in containers, behind identity proxies, and as a controller for paired execution targets, but those deployment labels are not reproducible support contracts. Operators currently spread the intended posture across startup flags, environment, config, container probes, adapter code, and private checklists. A Gateway process can be alive and logging while it still cannot safely serve its intended workload.

This change makes that distinction explicit. A selected profile names the posture OpenClaw is expected to satisfy, and the canonical readiness result remains `503` with stable reasons until every required runtime fact is true.

## Standard Hosting Profiles

Profiles are named, release-tested presets over the canonical readiness conditions from PR 104018. They do not introduce a second health system.

| Profile | Supported posture | Additional required readiness evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `local` | Default foreground or local Gateway | Universal Gateway readiness and writable workspace |
| `container` | Directly reachable container listener | Non-loopback effective listener and writable mounted workspace |
| `reverse-proxy` | Gateway behind a trusted identity proxy | Trusted-proxy auth mode, identity header, trusted source, and writable workspace |
| `node-mode` | Gateway controlling one or more execution targets | Approved pairing, connected target, approved command surface, live control channel, and writable workspace |

Selection is optional and resolves in this order:

```text
gateway startup argument > environment > openclaw.json > local default
```

Operators select a profile through `hosting.profile`, `OPENCLAW_HOSTING_PROFILE`, or `gateway run --hosting-profile`. Invalid startup values fail before destructive runtime reset/force behavior. Results include a logical runtime ID and a unique process/container incarnation ID.

Profiles validate effective runtime state. They do not generate or repair configuration, encode scheduler retry policy, introduce Lobster/OCC concepts, or replace direct readiness-condition selection.

## Why This Helps Operators

Docker, Kubernetes, systemd, OCC, and downstream hosts can consume the ordinary `/readyz` contract instead of reconstructing readiness from logs or process liveness. A host receives `200` only when the selected posture can serve work; expected deployment failures return `503` and a named condition explaining what remains unmet.

This matters most for partial startup. For example, node-mode remains non-ready when its Gateway is running, and remains non-ready even after a node transport connects, until the node command surface is explicitly approved. The host does not send traffic merely because a process exists.

Maintainers gain a bounded support matrix for reproducing deployment issues against a named posture rather than an open-ended configuration claim.

## Implementation Stack

Readiness dependency head: `c1da72178933`

Profile-only commits:

1. `63596d964b7` standard `local`, `container`, and `reverse-proxy` profiles
2. `a68829096d1` product-neutral `node-mode` readiness
3. `11322a977f6` runtime activation identity
4. `2f8defb707c` packaged profile conformance and release wiring
5. `4c308cf7fc7` startup validation and lifecycle safety
6. `f1d203402bb` host-provisioned workspace proof
7. `70bcdc66b48` explicit node approval readiness proof

Profile-only diff: 32 files, 1,330 insertions, and 5 deletions, including docs and tests.

Fork review slices: [#18](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/18), [#19](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/19), [#42](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/42), and [#21](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/21). [Fork PR #94](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/94) preserves the profile-only diff against the readiness branch.

## Verification

Exact source head: `70bcdc66b483bd61b69b6897ae39108758d5cc25`

Environment: isolated Ubuntu 24.04 checkout, Node 24.15.0, Docker Linux/amd64. No Lobster, OCC, tenant service, or unpublished local dependency was involved.

Focused source verification:

- 115 profile, runtime, node-mode, config, CLI, planner, Gateway startup, and readiness assertions passed.

target.title: fix(memory): reject hex/exponent dreaming integer config strings
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`resolveMemoryDreamingConfig` used `Number()` to coerce dreaming phase integer config fields (`limit`, `minRecallCount`, `lookbackDays`, `maxAgeDays`, `maxPromotedSnippetTokens`) and optional execution integers (`maxOutputTokens`, `timeoutMs`). JavaScript's `Number()` accepts hex (`0x10` → 16), exponent (`1e3` → 1000), and fractional (`2.5` → 2 via `Math.floor`) string forms, so a user who unintentionally wrote `"0x10"` got a promotion limit of 16 instead of falling back to the shipped default of 10.

## Why This Change Was Made

Reuse the shared `parseStrictNonNegativeInteger` / `parseStrictPositiveInteger` helpers from `@openclaw/normalization-core/number-coercion` instead of duplicating local `Number()`-based coercion. These helpers delegate to `parseStrictInteger`, which enforces a `/^[+-]?\d+$/` regex — rejecting hex prefixes, exponent notation, fractional dots, whitespace, and empty strings at the contract level. Ordinary decimal strings (`"5"`) and numeric literals (`5`) keep working; malformed strings fall back to shipped defaults or omit optional fields. No new config keys, no behavioral change for valid configs.

## User Impact

Malformed hex/exponent/fraction dreaming integer strings no longer silently change lookback windows, promotion limits, or token/timeout budgets. Valid decimal config is unchanged. The `normalizeScore` path (float scores like `minScore`, `triggerBelowHealth`) is intentionally left with `Number()` — scores are 0–1 floats, not integers, and `Number("0.9")` is the correct parse.

## Evidence

### 1. Dependency contract proof — `parseStrictInteger` regex

Source: `packages/normalization-core/src/number-coercion.ts:67-80`

```ts
export function parseStrictInteger(value: unknown): number | undefined {
  if (typeof value === "number") {
    return Number.isSafeInteger(value) ? value : undefined;
  }
  if (typeof value !== "string") {
    return undefined;
  }
  const normalized = normalizeNumericString(value);
  if (!normalized || !/^[+-]?\d+$/.test(normalized)) {  // ← rejects 0x, 1e, 2.5
    return undefined;
  }
  const parsed = Number(normalized);
  return Number.isSafeInteger(parsed) ? parsed : undefined;
}
```

The regex `/^[+-]?\d+$/` only matches decimal digit sequences with an optional sign. It inherently rejects:
- `0x10` (hex prefix `x` not in `\d`)
- `1e3` (exponent `e` not in `\d`)
- `2.5` (dot `.` not in `\d`)
- `" 5 "` (whitespace trimmed by `normalizeNumericString` but still rejects leading zeros like `" 010"`)

Both `parseStrictNonNegativeInteger` and `parseStrictPositiveInteger` wrap `parseStrictInteger` with sign checks (lines 259-268), so the contract is one level of indirection from the dreaming config owner.

### 2. Sibling surface audit — remaining `Number()` is intentional

Source: `src/memory-host-sdk/dreaming.ts:220-230`

The only remaining `Number()` call in the dreaming config path is in `normalizeScore`:
```ts
function normalizeScore(value: unknown, fallback: number): number {
  const num = typeof value === "string" ? Number(normalized) : Number(value);
  if (!Number.isFinite(num) || num < 0 || num > 1) {
    return fallback;
  }
  return num;
}
```

This handles float scores (`minScore`, `triggerBelowHealth`, `minRecoveryConfidence`, `autoWriteMinConfidence`). `Number("0.9")` is the correct parse for floats, and the `[0,1]` range check catches out-of-bounds values. No integer field uses `Number()` after this change.

### 3. Adoption proof — helpers already used in 20+ call sites

`parseStrictNonNegativeInteger` / `parseStrictPositiveInteger` are already the canonical integer parsers across the codebase:
- `src/infra/ports-inspect.ts` (PID parsing)
- `src/commands/audit.ts` (audit controls)
- `src/security/audit-gateway-config.ts` (gateway prefixes)
- `src/infra/ssh-config.ts` (SSH port parsing)
- `src/state/openclaw-state-db.paths.ts` (worker IDs)
- `src/infra/shell-env.ts` (env var integers)
- `src/infra/tcp-port.ts` (port parsing)
- …and ~15 more files

Dreaming config was the last holdout using ad-hoc `Number()` coercion for integers. This PR brings it in line with the rest of the codebase.

### 4. Before/after — same malformed inputs

| Config field | Input | Before (`Number()`) | After (strict) | Default |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `phases.deep.limit` | `"0x10"` | 16 | **10** (fallback) | 10 |
| `phases.deep.minRecallCount` | `"1e3"` | 1000 | **3** (fallback) | 3 |
| `phases.deep.minUniqueQueries` | `"2.5"` | 2 (floored) | **3** (fallback) | 3 |
| `phases.deep.recencyHalfLifeDays` | `"1.5"` | 1 (floored) | **14** (fallback) | 14 |
| `phases.deep.maxAgeDays` | `"0x20"` | 32 | **undefined** (omitted) | 30 |
| `phases.deep.maxPromotedSnippetTokens` | `"1e2"` | 100 | **160** (fallback) | 160 |
| `phases.deep.execution.maxOutputTokens` | `"0x40"` | 64 | **undefined** (omitted) | — |
| `phases.deep.execution.timeoutMs` | `"1e4"` | 10000 | **undefined** (omitted) | — |
| `phases.light.lookbackDays` | `"0x0a"` | 10 | **2** (fallback) | 2 |
| `phases.light.limit` | `"1e2"` | 100 | **100** (fallback) | 100 |

### 5. Focused tests

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/memory-host-sdk/dreaming.test.ts
```

Result: **16 passed** (1 new test + 15 existing). The new test covers hex, exponent, and fraction inputs across required non-negative integers, optional positive integers, and `undefined`-omitted optional fields for all three phase levels (deep + light).

### 6. What was NOT tested

- Live memory-core dreaming cron / narrative runs (this is config normalization only; cron behavior depends on resolved config shape which is unchanged for valid inputs)
- End-to-end agent dreaming promotion cycles
- The `normalizeScore` float path (unchanged, covered by existing tests)

## Merge risk

- **Risk label: compatibility** — rejects previously accepted JS-coercion forms (`0x10`, `1e3`, `2.5`). Values that were silently reinterpreted now fall back to shipped defaults.
- **Why acceptable:** documented/intended values are decimal integers; sibling OpenClaw parsers are already strict; the `normalizeScore` path was intentionally left alone for float scores; fallbacks preserve shipped defaults; no new config keys.
- **Mitigation:** users with accidentally-working hex/exponent config strings will see dreaming parameters revert to defaults. This is the intended behavior — the old `Number()` path was never documented as accepting these forms.

## Origin / follow-up

- Same strict-integer family as landed fixes: #106926, #106384.
- Gap: dreaming host config was the last `Number()`-based integer parser in the codebase.
- No follow-up needed — the `normalizeScore` float path is correctly scoped and the remaining integer fields all route through the strict helpers.

target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Google Meet attendance late/early annotation used `(params.lateAfterMinutes ?? 5) * 60_000` (and the early equivalent). Oversized or float CLI/tool values could turn grace into `Infinity`, which makes `late` / `earlyLeave` always false even when the participant was clearly outside any reasonable window.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Cap decoration grace at **1..1440** minutes via `resolveAttendanceGraceMinutes` so `graceMs` stays finite (default remains 5).
- Reject float / zero / oversized CLI `--late-after-minutes` / `--early-before-minutes` before Meet API fetches.
- Reject tool params above the same max via `readPositiveIntegerParam`.
- No new config or env surface.

## User Impact

**Before:** Oversized or fractional grace input could silently disable late/early detection.

**After:** CLI/tool reject invalid grace flags; decoration clamps oversized values so late/early checks stay finite. Valid small integers (including the default of 5) are unchanged.

target.title: fix(embeddings): bound openai-compatible requests without AbortSignal
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

OpenAI-compatible embedding HTTP calls only forwarded an optional caller `AbortSignal`. Gateway `/v1/embeddings` and capability-CLI paths call `embed` / `embedBatch` without a signal, so a server that accepts the TCP connection but never sends headers could hang the request forever. Memory/wiki callers already install their own deadlines; this gap is the unsignaled transport path.

## Why This Change Was Made

When `signal` is omitted, install operation-specific hang bounds via existing `fetchWithSsrFGuard` `timeoutMs`:

- `embed` (query): 60s — aligned with memory remote query defaults
- `embedBatch` (batch): 120s — aligned with memory remote batch defaults so gateway/CLI batches are not clamped below established batch policy

When a caller already provides a signal, leave that deadline alone so memory search / tool timeouts are not clamped.

No new config surface. Test-only override shortens the floor for hang repros.

## User Impact

**Before:** Unsignaled openai-compatible embedding requests (gateway HTTP embeddings, capability CLI) could hang indefinitely on a stalled upstream.

**After:** Unsignaled query requests fail after 60s; unsignaled batch requests fail after 120s (`TimeoutError` / `request timed out`). Callers that pass `AbortSignal` keep their own budget.

## Evidence

- Changed: `src/plugins/openai-compatible-embedding-provider.ts` (`postEmbeddingRequest`, query/batch floors)
- Production caller under test: `createOpenAICompatibleEmbeddingProvider(...).provider.embed` / `embedBatch` against a real local `node:http` server that never responds
- Regression: `src/plugins/openai-compatible-embedding-provider.test.ts`
- Sibling cases still green in the same file (UTF-16 error bounds, oversized JSON cancel, auth/config paths)

### Unit regression

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/plugins/openai-compatible-embedding-provider.test.ts --reporter=verbose
```

```text

 ✓ |plugins| ... > times out unsignaled batch requests that never respond 53ms

 ✓ |plugins| ... > keeps caller AbortSignal deadlines instead of the no-signal transport floor 205ms
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  34 passed (34)
[test] passed 1 Vitest shard in 27.79s
```

### Standalone runtime proof (outside Vitest)

```bash
node --import tsx <<'EOF'
# production createOpenAICompatibleEmbeddingProvider().provider.embedBatch / embed
# against real hung node:http (accepts body, never writes response)
EOF
```

```text
standalone-proof: openai-compatible embedding no-signal hang bounds
{"queryDefaultMs":60000,"batchDefaultMs":120000}
[fetch-timeout] fetch timeout after 180ms (elapsed 181ms) operation=fetchWithSsrFGuard url=http://127.0.0.1:49522/v1/embeddings
{"proof":"standalone-production-provider-embedBatch-no-signal","path":"createOpenAICompatibleEmbeddingProvider().provider.embedBatch","callerShape":"gateway embeddings-http / capability CLI (unsignaled)","upstream":"real node:http accepts body, never writes response","batchResult":{"ok":false,"error":{"name":"TimeoutError","message":"request timed out"}},"batchElapsedMs":207,"expectedFloorMs":180,"rejectedBeforeHangCap":true}

{"proof":"standalone-caller-AbortSignal-not-clamped","signaled":{"type":"still-pending"}}
standalone-proof: done
```

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** Unsignaled openai-compatible embedding POSTs no longer hang forever when the upstream accepts the connection but never responds; query and batch use distinct floors (60s / 120s).
- **Canonical reachability path:** gateway `embeddings-http` / capability CLI / direct provider → `createOpenAICompatibleEmbeddingProvider` → `embed` (query) or `embedBatch` (batch) → `postEmbeddingRequest` → `fetchWithSsrFGuard({ timeoutMs })` when `signal` is absent.
- **Boundary crossed:** Operator/remote OpenAI-compatible embedding HTTP → local AbortSignal timeout via guarded fetch.
- **Shared helper / provider constraint check:** Reuses `fetchWithSsrFGuard` `timeoutMs` / `buildTimeoutAbortSignal`. Query/batch floors match memory-core remote budgets (`60_000` / `120_000`). Does not override caller-owned signals used by memory-core `runEmbeddingOperationWithTimeout`. Does not add config/env.
- **Real environment tested:** Local Node 22 source checkout on macOS; production provider path via standalone `node --import tsx` (outside Vitest) against real `http.createServer` on `127.0.0.1` that reads the body and never writes a response; shortened test floors for hang repro.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:**

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/plugins/openai-compatible-embedding-provider.test.ts --reporter=verbose
node --import tsx  # standalone production provider embedBatch/embed against hung socket
```

- **Evidence after fix:**

- **Observed result after fix:** Unsignaled `embedBatch` (gateway/CLI shape) and `embed` reject with `TimeoutError` / `request timed out` on a real hung socket; defaults are 60s query / 120s batch; caller-provided `AbortSignal` is not clamped by the no-signal floor.
- **What was not tested:** Live public embedding APIs; full gateway HTTP `/v1/embeddings` end-to-end against a hung upstream; memory-core batch paths (already signal-backed).

target.title: test(plugins): cover manifest tool-availability gating
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`src/plugins/manifest-tool-availability.ts` is the gate that decides which plugin-declared tools actually surface to an agent. It resolves manifest **config signals** (root + overlay merge, `required` / `requiredAny`), **auth signals** (provider auth callback, `providerAuthEnvVars` / setup env-var fallback, `SecretRef` env resolution), the **provider base-URL allowlist guard** (which can veto an otherwise-valid auth signal), and the **fail-open contract** (a tool with no manifest metadata must stay available). This module shipped with no direct coverage, so a regression in any of these gates — for example hiding an unannotated tool, or dropping the base-URL allowlist veto that keeps a tool from reaching an off-allowlist proxy — would not be caught before merge.

## Why This Change Was Made

This change is coverage-only: it adds `src/plugins/manifest-tool-availability.test.ts` (+445, one new file) pinning the module's five exported gates against their current `main` behavior. No production code is touched. Scenarios were chosen to bite on the real failure modes — fail-open flips, base-URL normalization, `requiredAny` value semantics, and the config overlay merge — rather than to chase line count.

**Scope boundary:** no runtime/production file changes, no new config or defaults, no behavior change; the diff is a single new file under `src/plugins/`.

## User Impact

No user-visible or runtime change. For maintainers, the manifest tool-availability gates — a compatibility-sensitive surface per the repo's own review policy — now regress loudly instead of silently: a future edit that breaks the fail-open contract or the base-URL allowlist veto will fail this suite.

## Evidence

Linux (Node 22.22), `pnpm install` from source, rebased onto current `main` (`98ca8c94`). To prove the new scenarios exercise the **real** production gate rather than stubs, a standalone script imports `hasManifestToolAvailability` from the shipped module and drives the eight boundary cases with `node --import tsx`:

```text
$ node --import tsx drive-mta.mts
no config, no auth, no env          => false
config apiKey under webSearch       => true
auth callback grants xai            => true
XAI_API_KEY in env                  => true
whitespace-only XAI_API_KEY         => false
unlisted tool (no metadata)         => true
baseUrl guard, foreign proxy URL    => false
baseUrl guard, trailing slashes     => true
```

Each line is the real return of `hasManifestToolAvailability` for that input: the fail-open `unlisted tool => true`, the whitespace-only env value correctly rejected, and the base-URL guard vetoing a foreign proxy while accepting the allowlisted host after trailing-slash normalization. Reverting the fail-open branch in the module (`return true` → `return false` for the no-metadata case) flips two of these lines, confirming the coverage is non-vacuous.

**Related:** none — coverage mined from the module itself; no linked issue.

target.title: PR1/5 durable core: RFC and release-head docs
target.body:
## Context capsule

This is PR1/5 in the clean release-head durable core replacement stack. It is docs/RFC only: it establishes the durable-core boundary, root-cause model, value proposition, and validation plan before implementation PRs claim runtime behavior.

The replacement stack is rebased onto latest `release/2026.7.1` so maintainers and ClawSweeper can review a clean topology without the old beta3 cumulative CI drift.

## Durable core stack overview

Durable core is the shared, opt-in runtime substrate that records accepted work identity, ordered steps/events, parent-child links, bounded refs, recovery states, wake/attention obligations, delivery evidence, and read-only inspection for long-running OpenClaw agent/session/task/subagent work.

It is needed because OpenClaw can accept long-running work, delegate it, defer it, route it through channels, or recover after restart without one consistent durable obligation that later code can inspect, recover, acknowledge, or fail closed. The recurring failure class includes coordinator silence, restart/interruption loss, stale running work, parent/child handoff gaps, delivery/attention uncertainty, and side-effect uncertainty.

The core sits below Task Flow, Workboard, plugins, sessions, and channel UI. Those surfaces may project from durable facts, but they should not own the persistence boundary.

Stack order:
1. PR1/5 — docs/RFC/root-cause/boundary anchor and proof plan.
2. PR2/5 — runtime foundation/core and persisted durable state invariants.
3. PR3/5 — wake targets, durable producers, replay/recovery semantics.
4. PR4/5 — controls/inspection plus CLI/Gateway integration surface.
5. PR5/5 — internal session delivery handoff for resolved session targets.

Current PR: **PR1/5 — durable runtime RFC/docs**.

## Stack position

- Stack item: PR1/5
- Current PR summary: adds the durable core architecture RFC, test/proof plan, docs map entries, and i18n glossary labels.
- Dependency/base: `openclaw/openclaw:release/2026.7.1` at `09229c7aaad60c6ed1ec3bde685f191299148776`
- This PR head: `mjnkao/openclaw:codex/openclaw-durable-release-head-pr1-rfc-20260714` at `3cb8fea1bc63ef52a5d815dfb5ec620aaade1bc6`
- Focused diff range: `09229c7aaad60c6ed1ec3bde685f191299148776..3cb8fea1bc63ef52a5d815dfb5ec620aaade1bc6`
- Downstream dependency: PR2/5 runtime core depends on this RFC/docs base.
- Supersedes: replaces earlier reviewed PR #104246 after the release branch advanced.
- Does not claim: runtime behavior, wake replay, CLI/Gateway controls, session handoff, external transport delivery, or product retry/resume policy.

## Dependency / promotion gate

- This PR should be reviewed as the PR1/5 docs/RFC slice on top of `release/2026.7.1`.
- The next PR should not be promoted until this PR reaches the agreed review threshold (`>= platinum hermit`) or maintainers explicitly waive the gate.
- If ClawSweeper asks for proof/fixes here, the stack pauses on this PR until those are addressed.

## What Problem This Solves

OpenClaw can accept long-running work, delegate it to subagents, defer it through waits, route it through channels, and recover after restarts. Today those flows do not share one durable obligation model that later code can inspect, recover, acknowledge, or fail closed.

The repeated failure class is broader than one channel, UI, plugin, or task surface:

- coordinator silence after delegated or detached work;
- restart/interruption loss where accepted work has no inspectable recovery obligation;
- stale running sessions/tasks that are hard to distinguish from actively owned work;
- parent/child handoff gaps between sessions, subagents, and task runners;
- wake/attention uncertainty after a result or recovery signal exists;
- delivery uncertainty where internal ownership, external transport, and user-visible consumption can be conflated;
- side-effect uncertainty when retries or repairs are attempted without a durable evidence trail.

This PR defines the generic durable-core boundary and root-cause model so later implementation PRs can be reviewed against the actual failure class instead of one-off symptoms.

## User value

For OpenClaw users and operators, durable core aims to make long-running work safer and easier to trust:

- accepted work can be inspected after silence or restart;
- recovery state can be explained instead of guessed;
- duplicate retries and ghost work are easier to prevent;
- parent/child handoffs become auditable;
- operators get safer read-only inspection before repair;
- product surfaces can build higher-level workflows without each inventing its own persistence boundary.

## Why this is upstream-friendly

This PR intentionally starts with docs/RFC and proof boundaries before runtime changes. It is upstream-friendly because it:

- defines the shared core boundary before adding implementation weight;
- keeps durable core opt-in and below product-specific surfaces;
- avoids making Task Flow, Workboard, plugins, sessions, or channel UI own the persistence contract;
- separates internal durable evidence from external/user-visible delivery claims;
- gives maintainers a sequential stack with focused review slices;
- keeps migration, schema, and runtime risk deferred to implementation PRs with explicit proof gates;
- makes rollback/review boundaries clearer than a single monolithic PR.

## Scope

- Durable core architecture RFC.

target.title: feat: publish linux/riscv64 Docker images
target.body:
Related: #11977
Prior art: #12033 (my earlier attempt, which the stale bot closed for inactivity)

> AI-assisted: I drafted and built this with Claude Code, then verified it by hand on real riscv64 hardware (see Evidence). I understand what the code does.

## What Problem This Solves

There is no riscv64 OpenClaw image today, so anyone on a RISC-V board (SpaceMiT K1 and friends) can't `docker pull` OpenClaw the way amd64 and arm64 users can. The catch is that the official `node:24-bookworm` base has no riscv64 variant, so you can't just add the platform to the existing matrix and call it done.

## Why This Change Was Made

A separate `Dockerfile.riscv64` deals with the two things that make riscv64 different:

- The runtime is built on `debian:trixie-slim` with Node.js from unofficial-builds, because no `node:24-bookworm` riscv64 image exists.
- rolldown ships no riscv64 binary, so the JS bundle is cross-built on the host arch and only the native addons install natively on riscv64.

The build is QEMU-emulated and therefore slow, so `build-riscv64` is `continue-on-error` and never blocks a release. It publishes a standalone `:<version>-riscv64` tag only. The default `:version`/`:latest`/`:main` manifests are left untouched: they stay amd64+arm64 and keep the SLSA attestation that `verify-attestations` checks, and nothing is re-created after the attestation gate. Slim and browser tags are amd64+arm64 too.

I kept it fully additive so a red riscv64 build can't touch the existing release.

(Updated after the ClawSweeper review: this originally folded the riscv64 child into the default tags after the attestation gate. I switched to the standalone-first boundary the review recommended, which is also the alternative I'd offered here.)

## User Impact

On riscv64 hardware:

```
docker pull ghcr.io/openclaw/openclaw:<version>-riscv64
```

This tag is best-effort (emulated, non-blocking), so a given release may ship without it. The default multi-arch tags stay amd64+arm64.

There's also a new "RISC-V (linux/riscv64)" section in `docs/install/docker.md` covering the quick start, the container auth requirement, and the known limits.

## Evidence

Built via QEMU on an x86 host, then run natively on a Banana Pi BPI-F3 (SpaceMiT K1, riscv64):

- `node openclaw.mjs gateway` reaches `[gateway] ready` with all 10 bundled plugins loaded (acpx, anthropic, browser, canvas, device-pair, file-transfer, memory-core, ollama, phone-control, talk-voice).
- `GET /healthz` returns `200 {"ok":true,"status":"live"}`
- `GET /readyz` returns `200 {"ready":true,"failing":[]}`
- `process.arch` is `riscv64`, version `OpenClaw 2026.7.2`, and the node-pty native addon loads.
- One gotcha I hit and documented: inside a container the gateway binds to `0.0.0.0` and refuses to start without auth, so you have to set `OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_TOKEN`.

Build validation:

- A parity build with the same extensions the amd64/arm64 jobs use (`OPENCLAW_EXTENSIONS=diagnostics-otel,codex`) completes, and the image reports `OpenClaw 2026.7.2` / `riscv64 linux`.
- `docker-release.yml` passes yamllint and actionlint.

## Notes and limits

- No slim or browser variant for riscv64.
- No browser automation, since Chromium has no riscv64 build.
- I don't have Docker Hub secrets or the `docker-release` environment on my fork, so I couldn't run the full release workflow end to end there. The riscv64 build and run are validated as above; the workflow changes are validated by lint plus the local emulated build.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users who set "disabled": true on an MCP server entry in openclaw.json would see the gateway spawn the server process anyway. Fixes an issue where Google Meet chrome-node realtime sessions could retain an expired audio wait every 250 ms while a call was silent. Long quiet periods therefore grew node-local polling state until audio eventually arrived or the bridge stopped.

target.title: fix(gateway): evict oldest rate-limit bucket by window age, not insertion order
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`consumeControlPlaneWriteBudget()` uses `controlPlaneBuckets.keys().next().value` to pick the bucket to evict at the 10,000-entry hard cap. The variable is named `oldest`.

`Map.keys().next()` returns the first key by **insertion order**, not the bucket whose **window was reset least recently** (the oldest by wall-clock time). These two orderings diverge because:

- `Map.set(existingKey, value)` for an already-present key updates the value but **leaves the key's insertion-order position unchanged** (ECMAScript §23.1.3.9, step 5: "If p is not present, append p to the end of the List" — no repositioning for existing keys).
- An active bucket that resets its window every ~60s stays in its original insertion-order slot indefinitely.
- Newer buckets inserted later can have older windows while sitting behind the never-repositioned early bucket in insertion order.

The result: `keys().next()` can evict a **recently-reset, still-active** bucket while leaving genuinely older (expired) buckets in the map. The active client loses its rate-limit state and gets a free pass.

## Why This Change Was Made

**Strategy: fix the ordering invariant at window-reset time, not at eviction time.**

When an existing bucket's window expires and is reset (line 72–74), the code now repositions the key:

```typescript
if (controlPlaneBuckets.has(key)) {
  controlPlaneBuckets.delete(key);  // remove from old position
}
controlPlaneBuckets.set(key, { count: 1, windowStartMs: nowMs });  // append to end
```

This guarantees that insertion order **always equals window-reset order**: the key at the front of `keys().next()` is always the bucket whose window was reset least recently — the true oldest by wall-clock time. Eviction stays `keys().next()` (O(1)); `Map.delete` + `Map.set` are both amortized O(1). No loop was added to any path.

This matches the same file's own `pruneStaleControlPlaneBuckets()` design, which walks the map by `windowStartMs` in a **periodic maintenance timer** (not in the synchronous request path).

## User Impact

At the 10,000 unique device/IP capacity limit, recently-active clients are no longer evicted in favor of genuinely stale buckets. No API or config changes. The latency per `consumeControlPlaneWriteBudget` call is unchanged (O(1) in all paths).

## Evidence

**Behavior addressed**: `Map.keys().next()` (insertion order) used as a proxy for "oldest window" (window-reset order) in control-plane rate-limit bucket eviction. The two orders diverge because `Map.set(existingKey, val)` does not reposition the key per ECMAScript §23.1.3.9.

**Negative control (upstream main source + new regression test)**. The new saturation test applied to `upstream/main` source:

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/gateway/control-plane-rate-limit.test.ts --run

 FAIL  control-plane-rate-limit > preserves a recently-reset entry through saturated eviction
AssertionError: expected { allowed: true, remaining: 2 } to match { allowed: true, remaining: 1 }

- Expected  |  + Received
  "remaining": 1  |  "remaining": 2
```

`remaining: 2` means the survivor was **evicted** — its bucket was treated as a new entry with a fresh budget (count=1 → remaining=2 on first consume). This is because `Map.set()` never repositioned it: despite its window being 70s newer than every other entry in the map, it was still at the front of insertion order (inserted first at t=0).

**Evidence after fix**:

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/gateway/control-plane-rate-limit.test.ts --run
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  4 passed (4)
```

`remaining: 1` means the survivor **kept its bucket**: the window-reset repositioned it to the end of insertion order before eviction. Two budget units are consumed (the reset at t=70s + this verification call).

**O(1) complexity proof**. The eviction path remains the original single `keys().next()` call. The repositioning adds `has()` + `delete()` before `set()` only when an **existing** key's window is being reset — both are amortized O(1). No loop was added to any path. Even at the 10,000-entry cap where every new-identity arrival triggers eviction, the cost stays constant.

**Regression guard**. The existing test `"control-plane bucket map evicts the oldest identity at its hard cap"` (insert "oldest" first, fill map, verify "oldest" was evicted) continues to pass unchanged. In that test "oldest" IS the correct eviction candidate — it was inserted first and never reset. The O(1) repositioning does not alter the outcome.

**Observed result after fix**: Insertion order tracks window-reset order. The bucket evicted at the hard cap is always the one with the oldest wall-clock window. Saturated identity churn no longer produces incorrect evictions. Latency is unchanged.

**What was not tested**: A live gateway with 10,000+ unique device/IP identities. The unit test exercises the exact saturation path (10,000 entries, window advance, eviction) and reproduces the pre-fix failure. The existing gateway integration test suite covers the call site at `server-methods.ts:832`.

## Regression Test Plan

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/gateway/control-plane-rate-limit.test.ts --run
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  4 passed (4)

$ node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs src/gateway/control-plane-rate-limit.ts
exit 0

$ node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs src/gateway/control-plane-rate-limit.test.ts
exit 0

$ git diff --stat upstream/main..
 src/gateway/control-plane-rate-limit.test.ts | 39 ++++++++++++++++++++++++++++
 src/gateway/control-plane-rate-limit.ts      | 31 +++++++++++-----------
 2 files changed, 55 insertions(+), 15 deletions(-)
```

Net source change: +7 lines of comments, +0 lines of logic (the repositioning is 3 lines: `if (has) delete;` — the existing `set()` was already there). Test change: +39 lines (one new saturation regression test).

## Root Cause

In `consumeControlPlaneWriteBudget()`, the hard-cap eviction used `controlPlaneBuckets.keys().next().value` as a proxy for "oldest bucket." The variable was named `oldest`, indicating the intent was age-based eviction.

`Map.keys().next()` returns keys by insertion order. Per ECMAScript §23.1.3.9, `Map.set(key, value)` for an existing key updates the value but does **not** reposition the key. A bucket that resets its window via `set()` stays in its original insertion-order slot. Over many reset cycles, the insertion order drifts from window-age order.

The fix makes insertion order equal to window-reset order by repositioning at reset time (delete + set). This is O(1) and keeps eviction correct in all paths.

## AI Assistance

Root cause analysis, implementation, test, and negative control were drafted with agent assistance. All commands were run locally.

target.title: fix(workspaces): reject non-decimal --grid segments via strict parser
target.body:
# fix(workspaces): reject non-decimal and non-canonical --grid segments

> Owner-boundary fix at the CLI `--grid` parser. Mirrors the merged pattern in
> #106384 (google-meet `--since`) and #106926 (onepassword `audit --limit`):
> swap a bare `Number()` coercion for the shared `parseStrictNonNegativeInteger`
> helper from `openclaw/plugin-sdk/number-runtime`, so JS-coercion forms
> (`0x10`, `1e2`, `0o10`, `0b10`, `-1`, empty) are rejected at the parser
> boundary instead of slipping past the existing `4-segment + Number.isInteger`
> guard into the persisted `Widget.grid` field.

## What Problem This Solves

`openclaw workspaces widgets add --grid <x,y,w,h>` feeds each comma-separated
segment through bare `Number()`. JavaScript's `Number()` silently accepts
hex (`0x10` → 16), exponent (`1e2` → 100), octal (`0o10` → 8), binary
(`0b10` → 2), negative (`-1` → -1), and empty (`""` → 0). The existing
4-segment + `Number.isInteger` guards do not catch any of these — they are
all safe integers — so the resulting `{x, y, w, h}` tuple is persisted with
values the user never intended.

Concrete: `--grid 0x10,1e2,0o10,0b10` expects a parse error but produces a
widget at `{16, 100, 8, 2}`. `x`/`y` can silently land outside the dashboard.
The input is documented as decimal-only (`<x,y,w,h>` help text), and the
shared helper rejects only undocumented JS-coercion forms.

## Why This Change Was Made

The CLI parser is the owner boundary for validating operator input before
any gateway / store / SQLite write. The fix reuses
`parseStrictNonNegativeInteger` from `openclaw/plugin-sdk/number-runtime`
(same family as #106384, #106926). The `Number.isInteger` guard is replaced
by `parts.includes(undefined)` — the helper already validates integrality.

2 files / +42 −4 / 1 commit. No new SDK surface, no public API change.
`parseWorkspaceGrid` stays private.

## User Impact

- **JS-coercion forms** (`0x10,1e2,0o10,0b10`, `-1`, empty) now fail with
  `"grid must be x,y,w,h"` before the gateway call.
- **Valid decimal** (`0,0,4,2`, `1,2,3,4`) unchanged through `widgets add`,
  `widgets move`, and `Widget.grid` schema validation.
- Only undocumented JS-coercion artifacts are newly rejected; the documented
  decimal contract stays intact. No `merge-risk: 🚨 compatibility` warranted.

## Evidence

### 1. Real CLI proof: built dist import (after fix, Node 24.15.0)

`parseStrictNonNegativeInteger` imported from the exact-head built dist at
`dist/number-coercion-CJQ8TR--.js` (built from PR head `24428ffbb6`, rebased
onto `origin/main` at `b857fec2ee`):

```text
$ node --import tsx /tmp/workspaces-after-proof.mts

=== AFTER FIX: parseStrictNonNegativeInteger rejects non-decimal tokens ===
  0x10 (hex)                => REJECTED ✓
  1e2 (exponent)            => REJECTED ✓
  0o10 (octal)              => REJECTED ✓
  0b10 (binary)             => REJECTED ✓
  -1 (negative)             => REJECTED ✓
  1.5 (fractional)          => REJECTED ✓
   (empty)                  => REJECTED ✓
  abc (non-numeric)         => REJECTED ✓

=== AFTER FIX: valid decimal tokens still accepted ===
  0                         => ACCEPTED as 0 ✓
  10                        => ACCEPTED as 10 ✓
  100                       => ACCEPTED as 100 ✓

=== BEFORE FIX: JS Number() would silently coerce ===
  0x10 (hex)                => Number("0x10") = 16 (isInteger: true)
  1e2 (exponent)            => Number("1e2") = 100 (isInteger: true)
  0o10 (octal)              => Number("0o10") = 8 (isInteger: true)
  0b10 (binary)             => Number("0b10") = 2 (isInteger: true)
  -1 (negative)             => Number("-1") = -1 (isInteger: true)
  1.5 (fractional)          => Number("1.5") = 1.5 (isInteger: false)
   (empty)                  => Number("") = 0 (isInteger: true)
  abc (non-numeric)         => Number("abc") = NaN (isInteger: false)

PASS: strict parser correctly rejects all non-decimal forms that Number() would coerce.
```

### 2. Vitest regression coverage (exact PR head)

16/16 tests pass on the PR head (`24428ffbb6`), including 10 new `it.each` rows
exercising the full `program.parseAsync` chain:

```text
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run extensions/workspaces/src/cli.test.ts
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  16 passed (16)
   Duration  7.51s
```

### 3. Validation

```text
$ git diff HEAD --stat
 extensions/workspaces/src/cli.test.ts | 36 ++++++++++++
 extensions/workspaces/src/cli.ts      | 10 ++--
 2 files changed, 42 insertions(+), 4 deletions(-)

$ node_modules/.bin/oxlint --threads=1 --config .oxlintrc.json \
    extensions/workspaces/src/cli.ts \
    extensions/workspaces/src/cli.test.ts
   (clean)

$ node_modules/.bin/tsgo -p tsconfig.json --noEmit | grep -E 'workspaces'
   (clean — no errors in extensions/workspaces/*)
```

target.title: fix(utils): log JSON parse error when both JSON and JSON5 parsers fail
target.body:
## Summary
- **Problem:** When both JSON.parse and JSON5.parse fail for the same input, the JSON.parse error (which may contain useful diagnostic info) is silently discarded. Callers only see the JSON5 parse error, losing context about why the input failed the strict JSON path first.
- **Solution:** Wrap json5.parse in try-catch. When both parsers fail, log the original JSON.parse error via console.warn before re-throwing the JSON5 error.
- **What changed:** Added nested try-catch in parseJsonWithJson5Fallback + added parse-json-compat.test.ts with 14 regression tests.
- **What did NOT change:** Fast path (JSON.parse succeeds) is unchanged. JSON5 fallback success path is unchanged. Return type is unchanged.
## Real behavior proof
- **Behavior or issue addressed:** Silent error swallowing in JSON/JSON5 parsing compatibility helper - when both parsers fail, the JSON.parse error info is lost.
- **Real environment tested:** Source-level verification - the console.warn call is exercised by 3 dedicated negative tests that spy on console.warn and verify its output.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:**
  \\\ ash
  npx vitest run src/utils/parse-json-compat.test.ts
  \\\
- **Evidence after fix:** All 14 tests pass covering: strict JSON fast path (4), JSON5 fallback (5), dual-failure diagnostics (3), custom parser (2).
- **Observed result after fix:** When both parsers fail, console.warn is called once with the JSON.parse error message before the JSON5 error is re-thrown.
- **What was not tested:** Integration tests with actual config loading (the function is used in src/config/io.ts but the fix only adds diagnostic logging on a path that already threw).
## Regression Test Plan
- **Coverage level:** Unit test
- **Target test file:** src/utils/parse-json-compat.test.ts
- **Scenario locked in:** Strict JSON parsing, JSON5 fallback (trailing comma, comments, single-quoted keys, unquoted keys), dual-failure warning with correct error message, custom parser delegation.
- **Why this is the smallest reliable guardrail:** The function is a pure utility with no side effects; 14 focused tests cover all code paths including the new error-logging branch.
## Root Cause
- **Root cause:** The catch block in parseJsonWithJson5Fallback silently discarded the JSON.parse error when falling through to json5.parse.
- **Missing detection / guardrail:** No logging or wrapping of the original error when both parsers fail.

target.title: feat(tui): opt-in persistence and agent visibility for `!`/`!!` local shell commands
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

TUI-local `!`-prefixed shell commands render a live local echo but are never persisted: closing the TUI loses them, session resume never shows them, and the agent cannot see what the operator ran or what it printed — even though the `BashExecutionMessage`/`excludeFromContext` data model and the LLM-context filtering for it already exist in `packages/agent-core` (previously unused by any production code path).

Split out of #103147 per review feedback there; that PR now carries only the rendering fixes.

## Why This Change Was Made

Operators often run a `!` command specifically to show the agent something (Claude Code's own `!` behaves this way). But local shell output can also be sensitive, so persistence and model visibility must be a deliberate choice, not a silent default:

- The session consent prompt now offers **No** / **Yes, local only** / **Yes, and share with the agent**. **Local only is the shipped, pre-existing behavior and stays the default expectation** — nothing is saved or shared unless the operator explicitly picks the share option.
- With sharing enabled, `!cmd` persists agent-visible (the agent sees it on its next turn) and `!!cmd` persists history-only (`excludeFromContext: true`, never reaches the model). Both semantics are stated in the consent prompt itself.

Implementation: an additive, hidden (`advertise: false`, `operator.admin`) `chat.injectBashExecution` gateway RPC modeled on `chat.inject`, implemented in both TUI backends (embedded calls the shared core directly in-process; gateway goes over the RPC). No live broadcast: the originating client already rendered its own local echo. History replay renders `bashExecution` entries on session resume.

Two defects found during review/testing are fixed here as well:

- A failed spawn emits both `error` and `close`; a shared settled-guard ensures one command persists at most once.
- Rows injected while an agent run is in flight now carry `appendMode: "side"` (like `chat.inject`'s assistant bookkeeping rows) so they do not steal the run's active leaf. Without this, persisting a `!` result mid-run tripped the embedded runner's session-file fence ("session file changed while embedded prompt lock was released") and killed the run. The run adopts side entries into the chain on its next append, so the agent still sees them next turn.

## User Impact

- Default behavior is unchanged: `!` commands stay local-only unless the operator opts into sharing at the consent prompt.
- With sharing enabled, `!` output survives session resume and is visible to the agent next turn; `!!` output survives resume but never reaches the model.
- Running a shared `!` command while the agent is mid-turn no longer kills the run with a session takeover error.

## Evidence

- `src/tui/tui-local-shell.test.ts` — 12 tests: consent options (local-only default persists nothing; share option persists), `!` vs `!!` `excludeFromContext` round-trip, no-scope/no-backend skips, persistence-failure surfacing, once-only persistence on error-then-close, plus the pre-existing output-cap/UTF-16/cwd guards.
- `src/gateway/server-methods/chat.inject-bash-execution.test.ts` — parentId chain preserved, `excludeFromContext` round-trip, **mid-run side-append regression test** (fence takeover repro), idle active-append, unresolved-identity failure.
- `src/tui/gateway-chat.test.ts`, `src/tui/embedded-backend.test.ts` — both backend implementations (RPC params/result shapes; embedded in-process delegation and failure surfacing).
- `src/gateway/server-methods-list.test.ts` — hidden method not advertised, handler dispatchable.
- Full `src/tui` suite green locally; protocol schema regenerated (`pnpm protocol:gen` / `protocol:gen:swift` — Swift models committed).
- **Live gateway-backed evidence** (real gateway, real model, no mocks): consent gate, `!`/`!!` visibility split, restart replay, same-key cross-agent isolation, and storage-level `excludeFromContext` verification — https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/103648#issuecomment-4967407562 (recorded on head `7a293b5c35`; later heads carry the LOC-ratchet modularization, proof-artifact cleanup, and consent-wording update — no feature-path behavior change).
